messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Frank O'Donnell was seventy-six years old, a hotel manager for nearly four decades, and he had never thought much about chemicals until the morning a maintenance worker mixed bleach with ammonia in a utility closet on the second floor. The fumes bloomed through the hallway with astonishing speed—acrid, metallic, burning—and Frank, who had stepped in to check on a broken heater, inhaled deeply before he could stop himself. He remembered the instant seizing in his chest, the way his throat closed, the blind scramble toward the exit with tears streaming from his eyes. That was all that came back to him in a clear picture. The rest—being sprawled on the sidewalk, the paramedics, the oxygen mask—arrived in fragments that never quite formed a story. He would smell the chemical odor, sharp and cloying, out of nowhere while standing in his own kitchen, and his heart would race, his palms sweat, his whole body bracing for an attack that had already happened years ago. He could not call up an image of the closet or the hallway when the smell hit; the feeling came alone, without a picture, and that frightened him more than anything because it made no sense.

In the months afterward, Frank began to feel that his body had turned against him. His lungs still ached sometimes, the doctors said there was no permanent damage, but he could not shake the certainty that something inside had broken beyond repair. Every time his heart pounded at a sudden noise—a car backfiring, a dropped pan in the kitchen—he read it as proof that his body was still in danger, still fighting the fumes that were long gone. He started checking his own thoughts, too, scanning for the moment when his mind might finally give out, when the strange disconnected memories and the unexplained fear meant he was going crazy. He could not stop himself. The checking had become a habit by the time his wife left, though he understood why: she could not live with a man who jumped at every sound and insisted the only safe places were his bedroom and the corner grocery store two blocks away.

He put on loud music or the television at maximum volume in the afternoons because silence invited the smell or the fear, and because the noise drowned out his own thoughts long enough to let him breathe. He stopped going to the hotel where the exposure had happened. That part was easy at first—he had retired soon after, citing his age—but the avoidance spread. He no longer drove past that neighborhood. He stopped attending the hotel industry dinners where he used to network. He told himself it was sensible, that there was no reason to go near a place that had almost killed him. But the world kept shrinking. Even at home, inside his supposed safe zone, he felt alert and watchful, as though the chemical could seep through the walls or the loud music could trigger something worse. He only truly relaxed in two places: his leather armchair in the living room, facing the door, and the end of aisle three at the grocery store where he could see both exits.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in his own kitchen when he smelled ammonia on a clean countertop. No bleach had been used. No one else smelled it. He stood frozen, his body surging with adrenaline, and he realized he could not tell whether the smell was real or in his head. The uncertainty cracked something open. He had come to believe that bad things would happen no matter what he did—helplessness was a fact of life now—but this felt different. This felt like losing the ground under his feet. His daughter had been urging him for a year to talk to someone; he finally called. He was not hoping for a cure. He was hoping, at most, that someone might explain why he could feel the full force of that morning without any memory at all, and whether that meant he was already lost.
